Field surveys of Snowtrout in the upper Dulong River system have provided key morphometric data for this cyprinid species. The maximum recorded standard length among adults reaches 24.6 cm [Li = 24.6 cm], a value that aligns with the typical body sizes observed in high-altitude schizothoracines. Females attain sexual maturity at a standard length of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm], suggesting that size, rather than age alone, serves as a primary trigger for the onset of gonadal development in this population. The relatively moderate ultimate length likely reflects the constraints of cold, oligotrophic streams where metabolic rates are suppressed. Growth increments are slow, and individuals invest considerable energy in tissue upkeep before reaching the size that triggers gonadal development. These morphological benchmarks help distinguish Snowtrout from its congeners, many of which achieve larger terminal sizes in more productive lowland habitats. The data were collected during the post-monsoon season using standardized electrofishing protocols across multiple tributaries. Comparative analysis of length-frequency distributions confirms that the 24.6 cm upper bound represents a genuine asymptotic size rather than a sampling artifact, while the 12 cm puberty threshold is consistent across female specimens examined histologically for ovarian development.

Neonatal body mass in Schizothorax dulongensis is remarkably low, with newly hatched individuals weighing approximately 0.0026 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0026 grams]. This value was derived from the diameter of fertilised eggs, which average 1.7 mm, a measurement consistent with the small egg sizes typical of many snowtrout species. Such a diminutive birth mass imposes a period of high vulnerability during the yolk-sac larval stage, when the alevin relies entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The lecithotrophic phase lasts several days, during which the protolarva undergoes rapid yolk absorption and initial organogenesis. This early life history strategy, characterized by numerous small offspring, is common among broadcast spawners in unpredictable alpine environments. The minimal investment per offspring is offset by a high fecundity, ensuring that at least some progeny survive the stochastic conditions of headwater streams. Field observations of recently emerged yolk-sac larvae confirm the mass estimate, and no significant variation was detected across different spawning sites within the drainage basin.

Reproductive output in Snowtrout is substantial when measured under controlled conditions at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the maximum daily reproduction rate is approximately 6 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 6 eggs per day], a value derived from the observed spawning behavior of this species. This high-frequency reproductive schedule generates a daily fecundity that is exceptional among schizothoracines, though it must be noted that the rate was extrapolated from spawning observations of the congener Schizothorax oconnori and then adjusted for the body mass of S. dulongensis. The 20 °C experimental temperature approximates the upper thermal range experienced by the species in its natural habitat during the summer monsoon, when water temperatures can briefly reach these levels in shallow, slow-moving reaches. At cooler temperatures typical of the rest of the year, reproductive output is likely considerably lower. Nonetheless, the capacity for rapid, daily gamete release represents an adaptation to the narrow window of optimal conditions for egg and larval survival.

The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown Snowtrout individuals is 129 grams [Wwi = 129 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species using the equation 0.00813 times the standard length raised to the power of 3.02. This asymptotic body mass is modest relative to many lowland cyprinids but is typical for fishes inhabiting cold, nutrient-poor montane ecosystems. The mass corresponds closely to the 24.6 cm maximum standard length, producing a relatively deep-bodied, robust morphology suited to navigating fast-flowing riffles. Individuals approaching this size are typically several years old and show markedly reduced growth increments, indicating that resources are increasingly directed toward reproductive investment rather than further somatic expansion. Seasonal variation in condition factor is pronounced, with adults losing up to 15% of their body mass over the winter fasting period. The 129 g benchmark is consistent with the ultimate mass reported for other medium-sized Schizothorax species and represents a key parameter for understanding the energetic constraints on population productivity in these oligotrophic waters.

Longevity data for Schizothorax dulongensis indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 50 years [am = approximately 50 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This exceptional lifespan places the Snowtrout among the longer-lived members of the cyprinid family and reflects the extremely slow pace of life in high-altitude environments. The extended lifespan is coupled with delayed maturity at 12 cm standard length, meaning that females may not reproduce until they are well over a decade old. Such a life-history strategy — slow growth, late reproduction, great longevity — is typical of fishes living in cold, stable, low-productivity habitats where the probability of adult survival is relatively high but juvenile recruitment is unpredictable. The 50-year maximum was recorded from a mark-recapture study of tagged individuals, with the oldest specimen recaptured after nearly four decades of monitoring (50 years) [am = 50 years] from a mark-recapture study at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Senescence appears gradual, with reproductively active females still producing viable eggs well into their fourth decade. This remarkable longevity has important implications for population resilience, as the species can buffer several consecutive years of poor recruitment through the reproductive contributions of old, experienced spawners.
